title: HIV : to test or not to test?

sections.title: Page 1

summary.text: Opens a 1989 World Health Forum feature on whether to test for HIV, introducing a debate on the ethics of AIDS held in Geneva on the first World AIDS Day. A first speaker begins by distinguishing individual HIV testing, linked to an identifiable person, from population screening.

sections.extract: In Focus HIV—to test or not to test? World AIDS Day has been established as an annual event to be marked on 1 December each year. The first was held in 1988, when worldwide activities were coordinated by the World Health Organization (see Vol. 10, No.1, page 136). As part of the 24-hour event held in Geneva, a debate took place on the ethical aspects of AIDS. We publish below an edited version of part of the

summary.text: Continues the World AIDS Day debate, describing anonymous prevalence screening newly approved in the United Kingdom for monitoring the spread of HIV. The speaker argues that mandatory testing of individuals is costly and unreliable because tests can miss recent infection.

sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: Continues the debate with the view that public education is the cheapest and most effective way to control AIDS and that AIDS differs from diseases like tuberculosis where mass testing may be favoured. A further speaker endorses earlier views and turns to issues attracting public attention.

sections.extract: In Focus think the message that should go round the world from this World AIDS Day is that the cheapest, most effective control of AIDS is through public education. Most citizens have tuberculosis and other infectious diseases in mind when they think that mandatory testing of the whole population is the way ahead. summary.text: A speaker notes resistance in several countries to compulsory screening before marriage, during pregnancy or before surgery, and comments on public and press attitudes. The speaker raises the responsibility of people from developed countries who settle where others lack similar means of protection.

summary.text: Continues with the view that each case must respect both rights and responsibilities, followed by comments from Father Professor Carrasco on what happens once a person is identified as having AIDS. Another speaker argues that mandatory testing is an expensive and largely ineffective response given the heavy demands HIV will place on resources.

summary.text: Concludes the debate with arguments that mandatory testing risks serious discrimination, contrasting condom provision to prisoners in Switzerland with mandatory testing of prisoners in Australia. A closing quotation from C. Everett Koop calls for a unified global attack on AIDS.
